title: Measure for Measure
author: William Shakespeare
setting: Vienna: a palace, a nunnery, a brothel, a prison and a city gate
lengthNote: Around 2,800 lines, with the prison and brothel scenes largely in prose
openingLine: Of government the properties to unfold, Would seem in me to affect speech and discourse;
summary: A duke who has let the sexual laws lapse for years hands Vienna to a deputy known for severity, then stays behind disguised as a friar to watch what happens. Angelo condemns a man for getting his betrothed with child, and then offers the man's sister his life in exchange for her body. The comedy machinery — a substitution in bed, a substituted head, a public hearing — arrives on time and saves everyone it is supposed to save, and the play still ends with a marriage proposal that nobody on stage answers.

sourceText.label: Globe/Moby text of Measure for Measure
sourceText.note: Line numbers follow the traditional Globe numbering. The only early text is the First Folio of 1623, and modern editions vary by a line or two.

atAGlance.label: Written
atAGlance.note: The first year of James I's English reign, and the first full season after a long plague closure.

atAGlance.label: First recorded performance
atAGlance.note: Played at court during the Christmas season.

atAGlance.label: First printed
atAGlance.note: No quarto survives; the First Folio is the only early text, and some of its oddities are still argued over.

atAGlance.label: Chief sources
atAGlance.note: The Epitia story in Cinthio's Hecatommithi and George Whetstone's play Promos and Cassandra, in both of which the heroine yields.

structure.label: Act I
structure.title: Angelo in charge, and Claudio condemned
structure.summary: The Duke gives Angelo his authority in a scene of strange, clotted syntax, and announces a journey to Poland he does not take. Within hours a dormant statute has a man under sentence of death for fornication, and his sister is fetched out of a convent before she has taken her vows.

scenes.title: The commission
scenes.summary: The Duke deputes Angelo, with Escalus as his second, and leaves without explanation.

scenes.title: Vienna hears the news
scenes.summary: Lucio and the bawds learn that the brothels in the suburbs are to be pulled down; Claudio is led to prison.

scenes.title: The friar's cell
scenes.summary: The Duke admits he let the laws sleep for fourteen years and explains why he wants someone else to wake them.

scenes.title: The nunnery
scenes.summary: Isabella asks for a stricter rule; Lucio arrives and sends her to plead for her brother's life.

structure.label: Act II
structure.title: Isabella pleads, and Angelo names his price
structure.summary: Escalus argues for mercy and gets nowhere. Isabella argues better, and gets somewhere worse: Angelo discovers desire at exactly the moment he is being praised for having none. The second interview drops the metaphors and states the price.

scenes.title: The law and the constable
scenes.summary: Angelo refuses Escalus's appeal, then leaves him to a bawdy case that no court could untangle.

scenes.title: The first interview
scenes.summary: Isabella pleads for Claudio; Angelo refuses, tells her to come again, and is left horrified by his own appetite.

scenes.title: The prison
scenes.summary: The disguised Duke hears Juliet’s confession and wants to know whether she repents the act or the shame.

scenes.title: The offer
scenes.summary: Angelo names his terms, threatens to outweigh her word with his reputation, and gives her until tomorrow.

structure.label: Act III
structure.title: Claudio and Isabella, and the Duke’s plan
structure.summary: The Duke, in his friar's habit, prepares Claudio for death with a long argument that life is not worth keeping, and Claudio agrees until the alternative is named. Isabella's refusal is absolute and her brother's collapse is immediate. Out of that wreck the Duke improvises the bed trick, and the play's verse gives way to plotting.

scenes.title: Be absolute for death
scenes.summary: The Duke's consolation, Claudio's terror, Isabella's fury, and the first mention of Mariana.

scenes.title: The street before the prison
scenes.summary: Pompey is arrested, Lucio slanders the absent Duke to his face, and the Duke is left alone with a rhymed verdict on Angelo.

structure.label: Act IV
structure.title: The bed-trick, and the substituted head
structure.summary: A woman takes another woman's place in the dark and the law is satisfied by a technicality it was never told about. Angelo breaks his side of the bargain anyway and orders the execution brought forward, so a second substitution is needed; a condemned man refuses to be hanged, and a prisoner who has died of fever supplies the head.

scenes.title: The moated grange
scenes.summary: A song for Mariana, and Isabella's account of the garden gate, the keys and the appointed hour.

scenes.title: The warrant
scenes.summary: Angelo's message demands Claudio's head by four; the Duke persuades the Provost to disobey.

scenes.title: Barnardine will not die
scenes.summary: A drunk prisoner declines to be executed, and Ragozine's death of a fever provides a head instead.

scenes.title: Angelo alone
scenes.summary: He cannot understand the Duke’s instructions, and admits he would not undo the deed now if he could.

scenes.title: Letters
scenes.summary: The Duke, out of disguise, sets his return in motion.

scenes.title: Instructions
scenes.summary: Isabella is told to accuse herself of what never happened, and does not know why.

structure.label: Act V
structure.title: The hearing at the city gate
structure.summary: The Duke returns in his own person and judges a case in which he has already been every witness. He lets Isabella be called mad, lets Mariana be dismissed, and reveals himself only after Angelo has condemned himself twice. Four marriages are ordered, two of them as punishments, and the last question of the play is put to a woman who does not reply.

scenes.title: The city gate
scenes.summary: Accusation, disbelief, the friar unhooded, Angelo's sentence, Mariana's plea, Isabella's kneeling, Claudio alive, and a proposal.

characters.name: Duke Vincentio
characters.role: Duke of Vienna, disguised for most of the play as Friar Lodowick
characters.summary: He owns the problem and delegates the correction, which he admits privately is a way of avoiding the odium of enforcing laws he let sleep. As a friar he is everywhere, hearing confessions he has no right to hear and arranging the outcome scene by scene, and the play makes him charming enough that his manipulations take a while to look like manipulations.
characters.clue: He announces a journey to Poland, borrows a friar's habit instead, and spends the rest of the play eavesdropping on the government he gave away.

relationships.label: deputes and then tries
relationships.note: He suspects the outcome before he leaves; 1.3 says as much.

characters.name: Angelo
characters.summary: He is not a hypocrite when the play begins; he is a man with no experience of his own appetite, and he says so with something close to wonder the first time it appears. What makes him dangerous is his discovery that his reputation will carry any denial he chooses to make.
characters.clue: His blood is called snow-broth in Act I, and by Act II he is asking himself whether the tempter or the tempted sins most.
traits: willing to use his own name as a weapon

characters.name: Isabella
characters.role: A novice of the order of Saint Clare, Claudio's sister
characters.summary: She enters asking for a stricter rule than the convent offers and is immediately handed the most worldly argument in the play. Her rhetoric is the best in it — she wins every exchange with Angelo on the merits — and the same absolutism that makes her unanswerable on mercy makes her merciless to her brother twenty minutes later.
characters.clue: She asks the nuns for a stricter rule, out-argues a deputy on the nature of mercy, and calls her own brother a beast for wanting to live.

characters.name: Claudio
characters.role: A young gentleman under sentence of death
characters.summary: His offence is getting his own betrothed with child before the contract was made public, which is why the sentence looks less like justice than like a demonstration. He accepts death for about forty lines, and the speech in which he stops accepting it is the most frightened writing in Shakespeare about what being dead might be.
characters.clue: He is condemned for a child conceived with the woman he was already contracted to marry, and he changes his mind about dying the moment a way out is named.

characters.name: Lucio
characters.summary: He fetches Isabella, coaches her through the first interview and keeps the plot moving whenever it stalls, which makes his punishment at the end feel wildly out of proportion. He is also the only character who tells the disguised Duke what Vienna actually thinks of him, and the Duke never forgives it.
characters.clue: He is the one who tells a novice to go and plead, stands at her elbow whispering that she is doing well, and is later sentenced to marry a punk.

characters.name: Escalus
characters.role: An ancient lord, second in the commission
characters.summary: He is the play's picture of what ordinary good government looks like: he argues for Claudio, loses, and then spends a whole scene patiently failing to get a coherent account of a case out of a constable and a bawd. His reward for consistency is to be the last man in Vienna to learn what has been going on.
characters.clue: He observes that some rise by sin and some by virtue fall, and is still trying to run an orderly courtroom while a constable mangles every word he uses.

characters.name: Mariana
characters.role: Betrothed to Angelo, living at the moated grange
characters.summary: She was abandoned when her dowry was lost at sea and has been waiting ever since, which the play presents without comment as a normal consequence of a marriage market. Her plea for the man who wronged her is the moral turn of the last scene, and she makes it by asking Isabella — of all people — to kneel with her.
characters.clue: She lives alone at a moated grange with a boy to sing to her, and asks to keep the husband everyone else wants executed.

relationships.label: betrothed to, and married at the end
substitute for, and then suppliant to

characters.name: Pompey Bum
characters.role: A tapster and bawd, later assistant to the executioner
characters.summary: He wonders aloud whether the state means to geld and splay all the youth of the city, the sharpest question anyone asks about the new policy. Moving him from brothel to scaffold is the play's bluntest joke: the trade is the same, and the second one is legal.
characters.clue: He argues that his trade is lawful if the law will allow it, and ends the play learning to cut heads off instead.

characters.name: Barnardine
characters.role: A prisoner of nine years, condemned for murder
characters.summary: He is guilty, he is due to die, and he simply declines, which stops the whole machinery of the plot until a corpse can be found elsewhere. He is the one person in Vienna over whom neither the law nor the Duke has any purchase at all, and at the end he is pardoned without asking.
characters.clue: Drunk, unrepentant and nine years in gaol, he refuses to be executed on the grounds that he is not in the mood.

themes.name: Justice, mercy and measure
themes.summary: The title is a rule of equivalence from the Sermon on the Mount, and the play spends five acts testing whether human courts can operate it. Angelo applies the statute exactly and produces monstrosity; the Duke suspends it entirely and produces a city where liberty plucks justice by the nose. Neither extreme is offered as the answer.
themes.development: Escalus pleads proportion in 2.1, Isabella pleads mercy in 2.2, and in 5.1 the Duke pronounces an eye-for-an-eye sentence he has already arranged not to carry out.

themes.name: Authority and substitution
themes.summary: Everyone in the play stands in for someone else: a deputy for a duke, a friar for a deputy's judge, a woman for another woman, a dead man's head for a living man's. The play's political question is what happens to power when it is lent out, and whether the lender can ever really put it down.
themes.development: Angelo receives the commission in 1.1, exceeds it by 2.4, and in 5.1 is tried by the man whose authority he was using.

themes.name: Desire and the law
themes.summary: Vienna's statute treats sex as a matter of licensing, and the play answers by showing desire arriving where it was least expected, in a man who had built an identity on not having any. Angelo's horror is genuine; what he does with it is the crime.
themes.development: Lucio calls his blood snow-broth in 1.4; by 2.2 Angelo is asking who sins most, and by 4.4 he admits he would not undo the deed even if he could.

themes.name: Reputation
themes.summary: Angelo’s most chilling line is a statement of fact about testimony: his unsoiled name will outweigh her accusation, and he is right. The last act is built to prove him right for as long as possible, with Isabella dismissed as mad in front of a crowd before the truth is allowed out.
themes.development: The threat is made in 2.4 and executed in 5.1, where both women are publicly disbelieved by a judge who knows exactly what happened.

themes.name: Chastity, the body and exchange
themes.summary: Bodies in this play are currency: a maidenhead against a life, a marriage against a dowry lost at sea, a head against a head. Isabella's refusal is usually discussed as a moral choice, but the play frames it as a refusal to accept a rate of exchange that everyone around her treats as normal.
themes.development: The offer is made in 2.4, turned down in 3.1, and then satisfied in 4.1 by a substitution that pays with somebody else’s body.

themes.name: Silence and consent
themes.summary: The play's loudest moment is a gap in the text. Isabella has more lines than almost anyone up to Act V, argues her way through two interviews with a judge, and then receives a proposal of marriage and says nothing — twice. Whatever a production does with that silence becomes its reading of the whole play.
themes.development: She kneels for Angelo's life without being asked in 5.1, and then answers neither of the Duke's proposals; the Folio gives her no more words after her plea for Mariana.

techniques.name: The disguised ruler
techniques.definition: A governor who moves among his own subjects unrecognised.
techniques.inThisBook: The habit lets the Duke hear confessions, coach witnesses and edit the evidence, so the device that usually produces comic knowledge here produces a judge who has tampered with his own case.

techniques.name: The bed trick
techniques.definition: A substitution in the dark, in which one woman takes another's assignation.
techniques.inThisBook: Because Mariana was already contracted to Angelo, the trick makes his sin technically lawful and hers technically a marriage, which is the play at its most legally exact and least comfortable.

techniques.name: Shifts of register
techniques.definition: Moving between verse and prose to change the standing of a scene.
techniques.inThisBook: The great moral arguments are in verse and the cases that actually come to court — Elbow, Froth, Pompey — are in prose, so the law is heard twice, once as philosophy and once as a shambles.

techniques.name: Imagery of coin and seal
techniques.definition: Metaphors drawn from minting, weighing, stamping and testing metal.
techniques.inThisBook: Angelo is a name stamped on metal, virtues are coins that must go forth to be worth anything, and the bargain in 2.4 is transacted in the language of false coining.

techniques.name: Soliloquy
techniques.definition: A character alone on stage, thinking aloud to the audience.
techniques.inThisBook: Angelo gets the play's best ones and uses them to discover himself in real time; Isabella is given none, which is one reason her decisions are so fiercely argued over.

techniques.name: Dramatic irony
techniques.definition: The audience knows something a character on stage does not.
techniques.inThisBook: For three acts the audience watches people confess to, plead with and slander a friar they do not know is the duke, and in 5.1 that accumulated knowledge is used to make the audience complicit in a public humiliation.

quotations.text: Spirits are not finely touch'd But to fine issues, nor Nature never lends The smallest scruple of her excellence But, like a thrifty goddess, she determines Herself the glory of a creditor,
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Handing the commission to Angelo in the first scene.
quotations.analysis: Virtue is described as a loan advanced on interest, and the metaphor governs the rest of the play: nothing in Vienna is given, everything is lent, weighed or repaid. The Duke is also, in the same breath, telling Angelo that a reputation which is never spent is worthless — advice he is about to enforce experimentally.

quotations.text: Mortality and mercy in Vienna Live in thy tongue and heart: old Escalus, Though first in question, is thy secondary.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The formal transfer of power, with Escalus standing by.
quotations.analysis: Two abstractions are located in two organs, and the split is exact: death is something Angelo will say and mercy something he would have to feel. The last clause is the quiet cruelty — the older and better judge is demoted in the same sentence that gives the younger man the power of life.

quotations.text: so our decrees, Dead to infliction, to themselves are dead; And liberty plucks justice by the nose; The baby beats the nurse, and quite athwart Goes all decorum.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Explaining to Friar Thomas why he has let the laws lapse and why he will not enforce them himself.
quotations.analysis: This is the Duke’s own confession of negligence, made to a priest and not to the city. The two images are of insolence, a nose pulled, a nurse slapped, which suggests that what he fears for is the dignity of the law, not anybody’s safety.

quotations.text: a man whose blood Is very snow-broth; one who never feels The wanton stings and motions of the sense, But doth rebate and blunt his natural edge With profits of the mind, study and fast.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Lucio describing the new deputy to Isabella at the nunnery.
quotations.analysis: Melted snow is water that was once solid, so even the insult admits that something was made cold. Lucio is usually unreliable; here he is exactly right about the diagnosis and exactly wrong about the prognosis, which is the play's method with him throughout.

quotations.text: Our doubts are traitors And make us lose the good we oft might win By fearing to attempt.
quotations.speaker: Lucio
quotations.context: Pushing a reluctant Isabella to go and plead for her brother.
quotations.analysis: The line is quoted as encouragement so often that its context is worth keeping: it is a rake persuading a novice to leave her convent and go and bargain with a man for a life. 'Attempt' carried a sexual sense in this period, and the play will make that second meaning explicit within one act.

quotations.text: We must not make a scarecrow of the law, Setting it up to fear the birds of prey, And let it keep one shape, till custom make it Their perch and not their terror.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: The first words of his administration, refusing Escalus's plea for Claudio.
quotations.analysis: It is the best defence of enforcement anybody makes, and it is made with an image of birds settling comfortably on the thing meant to frighten them. Notice that Angelo’s argument is about how the law looks: he is worried about being laughed at, the same anxiety the Duke admitted in 1.3.

quotations.text: Some rise by sin, and some by virtue fall: Some run from brakes of ice, and answer none: And some condemned for a fault alone.
quotations.speaker: Escalus
quotations.context: Alone, after failing to save Claudio.
quotations.analysis: Three lines of rhyme dropped into a prose-heavy scene, marking a moment of private judgement in a public office. The chiasmus balances rising and falling so evenly that it blames no one, which is exactly the temper Angelo has just overruled.

quotations.text: Condemn the fault and not the actor of it? Why, every fault's condemn'd ere it be done: Mine were the very cipher of a function, To fine the faults whose fine stands in record, And let go by the actor.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Answering Isabella's opening argument in the first interview.
quotations.analysis: He is right, and the rightness is the problem: a law that punishes acts and not persons is not a law at all. 'Cipher' means a zero, so he pictures his own office as a nothing — and by the end of the scene he will have become exactly the actor he refuses to distinguish from the fault.

quotations.text: And mercy then will breathe within your lips, Like man new made.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: The climax of her first appeal: if he were in Claudio's place and Claudio in his.
quotations.analysis: The image is of God breathing life into Adam, so showing mercy is the moment a man becomes human at all. It is also the most physical thing she has said to him, and the speech that follows it is the one in which he begins to notice her voice.

quotations.text: O, it is excellent To have a giant's strength; but it is tyrannous To use it like a giant.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Pressing the argument after Angelo tells her that her brother dies tomorrow.
quotations.analysis: The sentence concedes the power before objecting to its use, which is why it works on a man who will not hear his authority questioned. It also states the play's political thesis in fifteen words: nothing here is wrong with the law itself, only with the scale at which a person chooses to apply it.

quotations.text: but man, proud man, Drest in a little brief authority, Most ignorant of what he's most assured, His glassy essence, like an angry ape, Plays such fantastic tricks before high heaven As make the angels weep;
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Contrasting divine thunder with the noise a magistrate makes.
quotations.analysis: ‘Glassy essence’ means mirror-like and also breakable, so the soul is a reflecting surface and something easily smashed. She is describing authority in general and has no idea she is describing the man in front of her; the audience, having heard him for a scene and a half, does.

quotations.text: What's this, what's this? Is this her fault or mine? The tempter or the tempted, who sins most? Ha! Not she: nor doth she tempt: but it is I
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Alone on stage the moment Isabella leaves.
quotations.analysis: The question is asked and answered inside four lines, and he gets it right: she does not tempt, and the fault is his. The play never lets him plead ignorance afterwards, which is why what he does in 2.4 is a decision.

quotations.text: Thieves for their robbery have authority When judges steal themselves.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Still alone, working out what his desire will cost the city.
quotations.analysis: He sees the whole constitutional consequence before he commits the offence: a corrupt bench licenses every crime beneath it. The line is also the play's answer to its own title, since a judge who steals has set the measure by which he must be measured.

quotations.text: Blood, thou art blood: Let's write good angel on the devil's horn: 'Tis not the devil's crest.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Waiting for Isabella's second visit, having found he cannot pray.
quotations.analysis: The tautology is the point: after a scene of argument he arrives at a fact that admits no argument. The heraldic image makes his own name a label that can be written on the wrong animal, and ‘good angel’ is one letter away from the name he signs on warrants.

quotations.text: I do arrest your words. Be that you are, That is, a woman; if you be more, you're none; If you be one, as you are well express'd By all external warrants, show it now, By putting on the destined livery.
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella has just said that women are frail; Angelo takes the admission literally.
quotations.analysis: He uses the vocabulary of his office to conduct a seduction — arrest, warrants, livery — so the extortion is phrased entirely in legal terms. The trap is grammatical: she conceded a general frailty, and he converts it into a personal obligation with the word 'now'.

quotations.text: Who will believe thee, Isabel? My unsoil'd name, the austereness of my life, My vouch against you, and my place i' the state, Will so your accusation overweigh, That you shall stifle in your own report
quotations.speaker: Angelo
quotations.context: Isabella threatens to tell the world what he is.
quotations.analysis: He does not deny that she could prove it; he explains that proof is not what decides such cases. 'Overweigh' returns the play to its scales, and in Act V the Duke will stage a hearing designed to demonstrate, at length and in public, that Angelo's calculation was accurate.

quotations.text: Then, Isabel, live chaste, and, brother, die: More than our brother is our chastity.
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act II, having refused Angelo's terms.
quotations.analysis: The decision is taken in a rhymed couplet, the form Shakespeare uses to close a scene and settle a question, so the verse itself insists that there is nothing left to discuss. She addresses herself and her absent brother in the same line, which is as close as the play comes to showing her weigh the two.

quotations.text: Be absolute for death; either death or life Shall thereby be the sweeter. Reason thus with life: If I do lose thee, I do lose a thing That none but fools would keep:
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: The disguised Duke preparing Claudio for execution.
quotations.analysis: It is a consolation built entirely out of contempt for living, and it persuades Claudio for about a hundred lines. The Duke knows at this point that he intends to save him, which makes the whole speech an exercise conducted on a man under sentence for the benefit of the man delivering it.

quotations.text: Ay, but to die, and go we know not where; To lie in cold obstruction and to rot; This sensible warm motion to become A kneaded clod; and the delighted spirit To bathe in fiery floods, or to reside
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Two words after agreeing that death is a fearful thing and shamed life a hateful one.
quotations.analysis: The fear is entirely physical until the fourth line, and the move from ‘warm motion’ to ‘kneaded clod’ is the whole argument: what terrifies him is the loss of warmth and movement. The speech begins with 'Ay, but' — a man conceding the philosophy and then finding it does not reach.

quotations.text: Sweet sister, let me live: What sin you do to save a brother's life, Nature dispenses with the deed so far That it becomes a virtue.
quotations.speaker: Claudio
quotations.context: Asking Isabella to accept Angelo's bargain.
quotations.analysis: He does not ask her to sin for him; he argues that in these circumstances it would not be a sin, which is exactly the reasoning Angelo used on her an act earlier. Hearing her brother speak in the deputy's voice is what produces the violence of her reply.

quotations.text: O you beast! O faithless coward! O dishonest wretch! Wilt thou be made a man out of my vice? Is't not a kind of incest, to take life From thine own sister's shame?
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Her immediate answer to Claudio's plea.
quotations.analysis: Three vocatives in a line and a half, each one shorter in patience than the last, and then a legal-sounding question that is not really a question. 'Made a man' is the cruellest phrase: she tells him that buying his life at this price would cost him his manhood as surely as it would cost her her chastity.

quotations.text: O, what may man within him hide, Though angel on the outward side!
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Alone at the end of Act III, in rhymed tetrameter.
quotations.analysis: The metre changes to the short, chanting line Shakespeare gives to choruses and spirits, which lifts the Duke out of the action and into the position of a commentator on it. The pun on Angelo's name has been waiting since the first scene, and it is sprung only once the plot to trap him is already in motion.

quotations.text: Take, O, take those lips away, That so sweetly were forsworn; And those eyes, the break of day, Lights that do mislead the morn:
quotations.speaker: A boy, singing
quotations.context: The song at Mariana's moated grange, which she breaks off when the friar arrives.
quotations.analysis: The only song in the play is given to the one character with nothing to do but wait, and she apologises for it immediately. Its subject is a broken oath, which is Angelo's offence against her five years before the plot begins, so the scene of the bed trick opens by reminding us who was wronged first.

quotations.text: I swear I will not die to-day for any man's persuasion.
quotations.speaker: Barnardine
quotations.context: Dragged out of his cell to be executed so that his head can be sent to Angelo.
quotations.analysis: A guilty man defeats the entire apparatus of the plot by declining to co-operate with it, and the Duke has no answer except to look for a different corpse. It is the one point in the play where authority, disguised or not, is simply told no and has to go away.

quotations.text: 'An Angelo for Claudio, death for death!' Haste still pays haste, and leisure answers leisure; Like doth quit like, and MEASURE still FOR MEASURE.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Sentencing Angelo at the city gate, after the marriage to Mariana.
quotations.analysis: The title arrives as a judicial formula in the mouth of a judge who has already prevented the death he is avenging. Everything in the line is balanced — haste against haste, like against like — and the balance is a performance, since Claudio is alive behind the scenes and the Duke knows it.

quotations.text: Let him not die. My brother had but justice, In that he did the thing for which he died: For Angelo, His act did not o'ertake his bad intent, And must be buried but as an intent
quotations.speaker: Isabella
quotations.context: Kneeling beside Mariana to beg for the life of the man she believes killed her brother.
quotations.analysis: She saves Angelo on a technicality of intention, not on a plea for mercy — the argument is that nothing actually happened, which she believes to be true. It is also the first time she admits that Claudio’s sentence was lawful, so her forgiveness of Angelo is bought by agreeing that her brother deserved to die.

quotations.text: If he be like your brother, for his sake Is he pardon'd; and, for your lovely sake, Give me your hand and say you will be mine.
quotations.speaker: Duke Vincentio
quotations.context: Claudio has just been unmuffled and restored; the proposal follows within three lines.
quotations.analysis: A pardon and a proposal are delivered in the same sentence, with the grammar making the second conditional on the goodwill created by the first. The Folio gives Isabella no reply here or at the second asking forty lines later, and every production has to decide what a woman does with a hand held out in front of a crowd.

timeline.label: Cinthio's Hecatommithi
timeline.detail: The collection containing the Epitia story, in which the sister yields to the magistrate and the brother is executed anyway.

timeline.label: George Whetstone's Promos and Cassandra
timeline.detail: A two-part English play on the same material, and Shakespeare's nearest model in his own language.

timeline.label: James VI's Basilikon Doron
timeline.detail: The king's own book of advice on rule, reprinted in London in 1603; its arguments about how a prince should hold himself were fresh when this play was written.

timeline.label: James VI of Scotland becomes James I of England
timeline.detail: A new ruler with known views on justice, clemency and the private conduct of magistrates.

timeline.label: Plague closes the London playhouses
timeline.detail: A long closure that pushed the King's Men out to the provinces and back to court performance.

timeline.label: The play is written
timeline.detail: Usually dated to this year, alongside Othello and the other so-called problem plays.

timeline.label: First recorded performance at court
timeline.detail: Played on 26 December during the Christmas season, before James I.

timeline.label: The Act to Restrain Abuses of Players
timeline.detail: Oaths and holy names were legislated off the public stage, one reason Folio texts of the period can differ from what was first spoken.

timeline.label: The First Folio
timeline.detail: The only early text of the play, printed among the comedies.

timeline.label: Davenant's The Law Against Lovers
timeline.detail: A Restoration adaptation that grafted Beatrice and Benedick onto this plot and gave the ending the romance the original withholds.

places.name: Vienna
places.note: The play’s setting: palace, nunnery, prison and city gate, imagined and not observed.

places.name: Whitehall, London
places.note: The royal palace where the first recorded performance was given at Christmas 1604.

places.name: Bankside, Southwark
places.note: The Globe's own neighbourhood of theatres, brothels and prisons, which the play's Vienna resembles more than any Austrian city.

places.name: Ferrara
places.note: The city of Cinthio, the Italian writer whose story of a corrupt magistrate lies behind the plot.

places.name: Warsaw
places.note: Poland is where the Duke announces he is going and where he never goes.

criticalViews.position: A Christian allegory of justice and mercy
criticalViews.summary: An older tradition reads the Duke as a figure of providence, the title as a text from the Sermon on the Mount, and the ending as a deliberate demonstration that strict law must give way to grace.
criticalViews.counter: It requires the Duke's methods to be above scrutiny, and the play goes out of its way to show him lying to a condemned man and to a grieving sister.

criticalViews.position: A problem play about power and coercion
criticalViews.summary: Twentieth-century criticism took the discomfort as the subject: an unresolvable case about consent, the abuse of office, and whether any authority in the play is exercised cleanly.
criticalViews.counter: Read only for its problems, the play can lose its comedy, and Pompey, Elbow and Barnardine are not incidental to it.

criticalViews.position: A Jacobean play about a particular kind of ruler
criticalViews.summary: Historicist readings set the disguised duke beside contemporary arguments about how a prince should show himself, govern through deputies and temper law with clemency.
criticalViews.counter: The parallel can flatter the Duke, since the play gives Lucio several hundred lines of unflattering gossip about him and never refutes them.

essayQuestions.question: Is the Duke a good governor?
plan: Start with his own account in 1.3: fourteen years of unenforced law, and an explicit wish to avoid being the one who enforces it.
Examine the friar's habit as a working method — confessions heard without right, evidence arranged, Claudio told he will die when the Duke means to save him.
Weigh what the disguise achieves against what it does: Mariana is rescued, and Isabella is deceived for two whole acts.
Read 5.1 as a piece of theatre he has scripted, and ask who it is for.
Close on the proposal, and on whether a governor who arranges his own marriage as the last item of a public hearing has understood anything he has seen.

essayQuestions.question: How does the play present Isabella's refusal?
essayQuestions.focus: Chastity, argument and the absence of soliloquy
plan: Establish what she is actually being asked for in 2.4, and in what terms Angelo phrases it.
Show her winning the argument on mercy in 2.2 and losing control of the situation for reasons that have nothing to do with the argument.
Set the couplet at the end of 2.4 beside her attack on Claudio in 3.1 and consider the difference between resolve and cruelty.
Note that she is never given a soliloquy, so the audience is denied the access it has to Angelo.
Test a modern reading against a Jacobean one: what does the play assume its audience already believes about a novice's vow?

essayQuestions.question: What is gained and lost by the bed trick?
plan: Explain the legal position: Mariana’s prior contract makes the encounter arguably a consummated marriage, not a crime.
Show what it saves — Isabella's vow, Claudio's life, Mariana's standing — and at whose expense.
Consider Angelo's position: he believes he has done the thing he is later condemned for, and 4.4 shows he does not repent it.
Compare the second substitution, Ragozine's head, and what the doubling of the device suggests about the plot's own methods.
Ask whether a device that resolves the plot without changing anybody's intentions can resolve the play.

essayQuestions.question: Why does the play end in silence?
essayQuestions.focus: The last scene, its marriages and its gaps
plan: Count the marriages ordered in 5.1 and note which are rewards and which are punishments.
Track Isabella's lines through the scene, from the accusation to her plea for Angelo, and mark where they stop.
Set the Duke's two proposals side by side and note that neither receives a spoken answer in the Folio.
Bring in Barnardine, pardoned without repenting, and Lucio, punished more heavily than the man who extorted a woman.
Conclude by judging whether the silences are a fault in an unfinished text or the play's last and hardest statement.

discussionQuestions: Angelo tells Isabella that nobody will believe her, and the last act proves him right for as long as the Duke allows. Why stage the disbelief at all?
Claudio is condemned for a child conceived with the woman he was contracted to marry. Does the play think the law is wrong, or only the sentence?
Barnardine simply refuses to be executed, and it works. What is he doing in the play?
Mariana asks Isabella to kneel with her, and Isabella does. Is that forgiveness, or exhaustion?
Lucio ends the play punished more severely, in his own estimation, than Angelo. Is the joke on him, or on the Duke?

related.why: Written within a year or so, and equally concerned with how easily a good name outweighs a true accusation.
The other play with a bed trick, and the other comedy that ends with a marriage the text will not make comfortable.
A courtroom in which mercy is argued for at length and then administered in a way that leaves the audience uneasy.
The preceding tragedy of a ruler who watches from behind a disguise of his own and stages a scene to catch a conscience.
Written a year or two later, and the fullest version of this play's question about what authority looks like from below.
